requirements.requirement: Run Prometheus on node1 and monitor node2, node3, and node4 through node_exporter on port 9100, identifying targets by node name.
requirements.summary: The validated configuration lists node2:9100, node3:9100, and node4:9100. Prometheus is active and enabled, its final API reports every named target up without scrape errors, and all three exporters are active, enabled, and listening on their managed IPv4 addresses at port 9100.

requirements.requirement: Make current host metrics from node2, node3, and node4 queryable on node1.
requirements.summary: PromQL executed on node1 returned exactly three identity and available-memory series, correctly mapping each instance to node2, node3, or node4. Freshness queries showed samples only 0.3–4.4 seconds old in the final audit.

requirements.requirement: Keep the Prometheus interface on port 9090 local to node1.
requirements.summary: The final Prometheus process listens solely on 127.0.0.1:9090, succeeds on local readiness checks, and cannot be reached from node2 through node1's managed address.

requirements.requirement: Limit every node_exporter endpoint to collection by node1.
requirements.summary: Before enforcement, peer nodes could reach the exporters. After enforcement, node1 successfully retrieved live metrics from all three endpoints while a different non-node1 peer timed out against each endpoint. Final nftables rules deny every IPv4 source other than node1, their drop counters incremented, and both exporter and guard services are active and enabled on all three nodes.

overall_summary: All material outcomes are satisfied. Direct final queries and network tests demonstrate healthy named targets, fresh metrics from all three systems, a loopback-only Prometheus interface, and node1-only access to every exporter.
limitations: Non-node1 denial was sampled using one peer per exporter rather than every possible source; the observed nftables rules explicitly cover all IPv4 sources other than node1.
No reboot was captured, so persistence is supported by enabled services and stored configuration rather than a reboot test; reboot durability was not explicitly required.
Lifecycle temporary-file inventories cover /tmp but not /var/tmp, so final cleanup of installation logs and status files cannot be confirmed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final lifecycle observations show no failed services or damaged dpkg state on any node, and the added listeners match the requested topology. Node1's unnecessary exporter service was disabled and left no port-9100 listener. A small deduction applies because installation log/status files under /var/tmp were still evidenced late in execution and no cleanup was captured.
